title: Horizontal Gaze Palsy: Clinical Mapping & Neuro-Ophthalmic Mastery
summary: Horizontal gaze palsy (HGP) is the inability to move both eyes conjugately in a single horizontal direction, signaling a lesion in the complex circuitry of the frontal eye fields or the pontine gaze centers. This guide provides a deep-dive into the neuroanatomy, etiology, and diagnostic nuances required for resident-level proficiency.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Core Concepts
sections.content: Horizontal Gaze Palsy is a conjugate ocular motility deficit where both eyes fail to move past the midline toward a specific side. Unlike a simple nerve palsy (e.g., VI nerve), HGP involves the 'yoking' mechanism. It results from damage to the supranuclear or nuclear pathways that coordinate the lateral rectus of one eye with the medial rectus of the fellow eye. It is classically divided into Cortical (Frontal Eye Fields) and Brainstem (PPRF/Abducens Nucleus) etiologies.

branches: Frontal Eye Fields (FEF): Generates contralateral saccades
Paramedian Pontine Reticular Formation (PPRF): The 'Gaze Center' for ipsilateral movement
Abducens Nucleus: Contains motor neurons (to LR) and interneurons (to contralateral MR via MLF)
Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF): Cross-brainstem connector to the III nerve nucleus
Superior Colliculus: Integration of visual and motor signals for reflexive saccades

rows: Eyes look TOWARD the lesion ('Wrong' side)
Eyes look AWAY from the lesion ('Right' side)
Intact (Eyes can be driven past midline by Doll's Head)
Absent (Eyes fixed, cannot be driven by Doll's Head)

sections.title: Essential Ocular Examination
content: 1. Observe Primary Position: Note any forced tonic deviation.
2. Assess Saccades: Rapidly move target between horizontal points.
3. Assess Smooth Pursuit: Slow target tracking.
4. Doll's Head Maneuver (VOR): Passive head rotation to differentiate supranuclear from nuclear lesions.
5. Caloric Stimulation: For comatose patients (COWS - Cold Opposite, Warm Same).
6. Bell's Phenomenon: Checking for vertical integrity.

sections.title: Red Flags: Urgent Neurological Threats
content: Acute onset with 'Worst Headache of Life' (Hemorrhage)
Ipsilateral facial nerve (VII) palsy (Pontine lesion)
Altered mental status or GCS drop
Papilledema (Increased intracranial pressure)
Contralateral hemiparesis in an elderly patient (Stroke)

branches: Structures: PPRF (or VI Nucleus) + Ipsilateral MLF
Movement: Only movement remaining is ABduction of contralateral eye

sections.title: HGP with Progressive Scoliosis (HGPPS)
content: Genetics: Autosomal Recessive mutation in ROBO3 (8q12).
Pathophysiology: Failure of crossing of somatosensory and corticospinal tracts.
Radiology: Deep midline pontine cleft (Butterfly sign).
Clinical: Complete absence of horizontal gaze + severe progressive scoliosis in childhood.
Note: Vertical gaze and convergence are typically spared.

rows: Variability, ptosis, and Cogan's lid twitch
Congenital, globe retraction, narrowing of palpebral fissure
Congenital VI and VII nerve palsies, limb defects
GQ1b antibodies, LP for albuminocytologic dissociation
Vertical gaze palsy, mid-dilated pupils, retraction nystagmus

sections.title: Imaging & Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. MRI Brain/Orbit: With and without Gadolinium. High-resolution T2/FLAIR for MS; DWI for acute stroke.
2. MRA/CTA: If vascular etiology (infarct/dissection) is suspected.
3. Lumbar Puncture: If MS (Oligoclonal bands) or Miller-Fisher/Meningitis is suspected.
4. Bloods: ESR/CRP (GCA in elderly), HbA1c, Lipids, RPR (Syphilis).
5. EMG/Jitter: If Myasthenia Gravis is high on the differential.

sections.title: Management Protocols
content: 1. Treat Primary Cause: Thrombolysis for stroke, Corticosteroids for MS or Vasculitis.
2. Prism Therapy: Fresnel or ground-in prisms to shift field if gaze is paretic but not totally absent.
3. Surgical Intervention: Large recession/resection or Transposition (e.g., Nishida) if stable and chronic.
4. Supportive Care: Patching for diplopia, Lubrication if VII nerve involvement (exposure keratopathy).
5. Physical Therapy: Especially for HGPPS patients with scoliosis.

content.explanation: PPRF (Pontine) = 'P' for 'Pushes' eyes AWAY from lesion. FEF (Frontal) = 'F' for 'Friend', eyes look AT their cortical friend (the lesion).

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Pearls
content: Foville Syndrome: Inferior pontine tegmental stroke causing HGP, ipsilateral VII palsy, and contralateral hemiparesis.
Saccadic Dysmetria: Often a precursor or subtle sign of cerebellar/brainstem involvement.
Skew Deviation: Frequently co-exists with brainstem HGP; look for vertical misalignment that does not follow a nerve pattern.
Thalamic Esotropia: Gaze palsy mimicking esotropia ('wrong-way eyes') can occur in thalamic hemorrhages.

sections.title: Foville Syndrome Breakdown
content: Lesion: Dorsolateral Pontine Tegmentum
VI Nerve Nucleus: Ipsilateral HGP
VII Nerve Fibers: Ipsilateral facial weakness
Verve Nerve (V): Ipsilateral facial anesthesia
VIII Nerve: Ipsilateral deafness/vertigo
Corticospinal Tract: Contralateral hemiparesis

sections.title: Recent Landmark Insights
sections.content: Recent studies in 'Nature Genetics' have elucidated the role of ROBO3 as a 'guidance receptor' specifically required for the crossing of axons in the hindbrain. In HGPPS, the failure of the superior cerebellar peduncles to decussate is now a hallmark radiographic finding on DTI (Diffusion Tensor Imaging). Furthermore, the use of Botulinum Toxin in the acute phase of stroke-related deviation is showing promise in preventing contracture of the antagonist muscles while waiting for neuro-recovery.
